subject: Physics
source: Paraphrased exemplars in the style of AQA GCSE Physics 8463 Papers 1 and 2 (2018 onwards). Stems are author-original; mark allocations follow published mark scheme conventions.

exemplars.stem: A car of mass 800 kg is travelling at 12 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car.
exemplars.markScheme: M1 for KE = ½mv². M1 for ½ × 800 × 12². A1 for 57600 J or 57.6 kJ.

exemplars.stem: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium is heated. The temperature rises by 25 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the aluminium.
exemplars.markScheme: M1 for ΔE = mcΔθ. M1 for 0.50 × 900 × 25. A1 for 11250 J or 11.25 kJ.
exemplars.source: AQA 8463 Required Practical 1 style — specific heat capacity calculation

exemplars.stem: A motor takes in 240 J of electrical energy and produces 168 J of useful kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage.
exemplars.markScheme: M1 for efficiency = useful / total. A1 for 168/240 × 100 = 70%.

exemplars.stem: A fixed resistor has a current of 0.40 A flowing through it when the potential difference across it is 6.0 V. Calculate the resistance of the resistor.
exemplars.markScheme: M1 for V = IR rearranged to R = V/I. M1 for 6.0 / 0.40. A1 for 15 Ω.

exemplars.stem: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series with a 12 V battery. Calculate (a) the total resistance, (b) the current flowing in the circuit, and (c) the potential difference across the 6 Ω resistor.
exemplars.markScheme: (a) M1 for R = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω. (b) M1 for I = V/R = 12/10 = 1.2 A. (c) M1 for V = IR = 1.2 × 6. A1 for 7.2 V.
exemplars.source: AQA 8463 Paper 1 style — series circuit calculations

exemplars.stem: Explain why electrical energy is transmitted across the National Grid at very high potential differences. Refer to power loss in your answer.
exemplars.markScheme: 1 mark: high pd allows lower current for the same power (since P = VI). 1 mark: power lost in cables is given by P = I²R. 1 mark: lower current means less power dissipated as heat. 1 mark: more efficient transmission overall.
exemplars.source: AQA 8463 Paper 1H style — National Grid efficiency (HT reasoning)

exemplars.stem: A regular cuboid of metal has dimensions 4 cm × 5 cm × 10 cm and a mass of 1600 g. Calculate the density of the metal in g/cm³.
exemplars.markScheme: M1 for V = 4 × 5 × 10 = 200 cm³. M1 for ρ = m/V. A1 for 8 g/cm³.
exemplars.source: AQA 8463 Required Practical 4 style — density of regular solid

exemplars.stem: Use the particle model to explain why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when its temperature is increased at constant volume.
exemplars.markScheme: 1 mark: particles gain kinetic energy as temperature rises. 1 mark: particles move faster on average. 1 mark: particles collide with the container walls more frequently. 1 mark: collisions are also more energetic, so force per unit area (pressure) increases.
exemplars.source: AQA 8463 Paper 1H style — gas pressure and temperature (HT reasoning)

exemplars.stem: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 4 hours. A sample initially has an activity of 800 Bq. Calculate the activity of the sample after 16 hours.
exemplars.markScheme: M1 for number of half-lives = 16/4 = 4. M1 for halving four times (800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50). A1 for 50 Bq.
exemplars.source: AQA 8463 Paper 1H style — half-life calculation (HT reasoning)
